title: The positive-pair graph defines what counts as the same scene
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: IMG-JEPA-01

TITLE:
The positive-pair graph defines what counts as the same scene

SOURCE:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — §§2.1–2.3, Figure 3, §7

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE] In the spectral setting, the learned directions come from the graph that positive pairs draw on world states. Exact agreement requires shared positives and uniqueness up to rotation. When the graphs differ, the bound depends on their mismatch and on the spectral gap.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The rule for pairing observations as a prior about which differences matter.

LOCAL MOVE:
The proof rewrites each modality’s learning objective on the same state space.

SOURCE TERMS:
Positive-pair distribution, world kernel, injective rendering, spectral gap.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] On Flickr, descriptions are grouped by photograph. The photograph supplies an address for the scene before the text encoder learns anything. Grouping by photographed event instead would change the learning problem.

QUESTION:
What does an imagetext experiment take as its unit of sameness: the image, the depicted event, or the relation a reader is asked to notice?

DEEPER QUESTION:
Can two descriptions of different images form a better pair for studying composition than two descriptions of the same image?

MECHANISM:
Changing the pair rule changes the graph. Under the paper’s spectral objective, this can change which distinctions survive in the leading embedding directions.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Observations> → <weighted edges between states> → [spectral embedding] → <geometry of learned similarities>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
Kπ = D^(-1/2) Π D^(-1/2), where Π represents the positive-pair distribution and D = diag(p). With second-order anti-collapse and a spectral gap, the solution is determined by the leading nonconstant eigenspace, up to rotation.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
NONE

TENSION:
The proof requires a specified relation among states. In imagetext analysis, deciding whether two views depict the same event can itself be an interpretive judgment.

MISSING:
A test that varies the grouping rule while holding the actual images and texts fixed.

BOUNDARY:
The spectral result supplies a sufficient condition for alignment under its assumptions. The paper leaves uniqueness under LeJEPA’s full-distribution constraint open.

CITATION TRAIL:
Laplacian eigenmaps and spectral contrastive learning, both cited in §2.1.

TEST:
Take one staged dispute photographed from several angles and a second dispute staged with the same blocking. Compare grouping by image ID, event ID, and blocking. Hold out one camera angle. Ask which grouping retrieves the same event and which retrieves the same composition.

PLATFORM:
[[Imagetext as a Unit of Analysis]]

LINKS:
[[Positive Pair Provenance]]
[[Scene Identity]]
[[Composition Across Images]]

title: A second description can inherit the first description’s omissions
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: IMG-JEPA-02

TITLE:
A second description can inherit the first description’s omissions

SOURCE:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — Appendix B, Table 7, §7

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE] At the 2.24M-image scale, alt-text paired with a text-only paraphrase scores .060 on WIT, against .055 for corrupted views of alt-text alone and .107 for the set using alt-text and two LLaVA recaptions. The recaptions carry information from prior image–text training.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
Whether a second text comes from looking at the image again or from rewriting the first text.

LOCAL MOVE:
Table 7 varies both the available descriptions and the rule for drawing positive views.

SOURCE TERMS:
Alt-text, recaption, paraphrase, good views, bad views, scene-explained fraction.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] Thick prompting can accumulate many sentences while remaining dependent on a single act of seeing. Conversely, two captions written by the same image model may repeat a learned convention even when both are produced from pixels.

QUESTION:
When a caption introduces a detail absent from the first description, how do we tell a fresh observation from a shared captioning convention?

DEEPER QUESTION:
How much of measured alignment comes from access to visible evidence, and how much from learning what caption writers tend to mention?

MECHANISM:
A paraphraser receives the first description. An image captioner receives visual evidence and brings its own training priors. Those are different routes for a detail to enter the second text.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Caption or photograph> → <input to a second describer> → [paraphrase or recaption] → <different evidence available for positive pairing>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
Log each description’s parent evidence: pixels, earlier text, or both. Independently mark whether each newly introduced claim is visible, contradicted, or undecidable from the image.

TENSION:
The caption source matters even under the paper’s bad-view rule. At the 50M-image scale, the two LLaVA recaptions with bad views score .092 on WIT, against .056 for alt-text with bad views.

MISSING:
A control that separates independent access to pixels from captioner conventions and differences in literalness.

BOUNDARY:
Table 7 supports effects of both data and view construction. Its rows do not isolate a causal effect of independent looking.

CITATION TRAIL:
Recap-DataComp, cited as [34], and the LLaVA caption provenance discussed in §7.

TEST:
For the same Shield of Achilles stills, collect one text-only paraphrase, one image-only description by a fresh observer, and one image-only description from a second captioner. Blindly verify every detail absent from the first text against the image. Count supported discoveries and repeated unsupported additions separately.

PLATFORM:
[[Thick Prompting as Method]]

LINKS:
[[Caption Provenance]]
[[Inherited Omission]]
[[Independent Looking]]

title: Viewpoint can be nuisance in a caption and instruction in a prompt
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: IMG-JEPA-03

TITLE:
Viewpoint can be nuisance in a caption and instruction in a prompt

SOURCE:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — §2.3

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE] “It is a nuisance only for alignment”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
A variable whose status changes when language moves from describing an image to directing its production.

LOCAL MOVE:
The authors distinguish the state a modality shares with others from observation-specific variation. They explicitly acknowledge that a camera-acting world model would need its viewpoint.

SOURCE TERMS:
State, nuisance, viewpoint, independent nuisances, alignment.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] An image encoder can benefit from treating two camera angles as equivalent for scene recognition. A prompt critic applying that same equivalence could reward a generator for ignoring an explicit camera instruction.

QUESTION:
Can an imagetext critic recognize the same depicted event across views while remaining sensitive to the requested view?

DEEPER QUESTION:
Who decides which details should survive alignment when the language itself selects what matters visually?

MECHANISM:
The positive-pair rule resamples viewpoint in the source model. A prompt such as “seen directly overhead” instead makes viewpoint a target whose value must affect the rendered image.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Camera angle> → <nuisance for scene recognition or constraint for generation> → [ignore or discriminate] → <different judgments of the same image pair>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
In §2.3, observations are g_m(z, ν). Good views draw independent nuisance variables ν and ν′; corruptions of one observation share its nuisance.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
Keep separate labels for event identity and prompt-constraint satisfaction. The same image pair may match on one and differ on the other.

TENSION:
A critic that strongly preserves camera geometry may mistake a viewpoint change for an event change. A critic that suppresses it may miss a visible prompt violation.

MISSING:
Instruction-conditioned evidence about which differences the critic should ignore.

BOUNDARY:
The paper’s nuisance analysis describes an alignment objective. Applying it to prompt compliance is an inference about a different task.

CITATION TRAIL:
§2.3’s explicit camera-acting example and §3.3’s tests of video frames as image views.

TEST:
Render the same dispute overhead and at eye level. Use both versions with “a dispute before elders,” then score both against “a dispute before elders seen directly overhead.” A critic passes if it preserves event identity in the first comparison and detects the wrong view in the second.

PLATFORM:
[[Operative Ekphrasis]]

LINKS:
[[Cinepromptography]]
[[Conditional Fidelity]]
[[Scene Identity]]

title: A prompt can change an image without making its meaning recoverable
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: IMG-JEPA-04

TITLE:
A prompt can change an image without making its meaning recoverable

SOURCE:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — §2.1, Appendix A.2, §7

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE] The proof uses the inverse of each injective rendering on its image. This lets the authors rewrite the objective over observations as an objective over world states. The limitations section identifies lossy real modalities as a departure from that setup.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The difference between a prompt detail having a visual effect and a viewer being able to infer that detail.

LOCAL MOVE:
Injectivity supplies recoverability in the formal model before learning begins.

SOURCE TERMS:
Injective rendering, left inverse, world state, population objective.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] Changing “blood-price” to “unpaid debt” could systematically alter a generator’s lighting or blocking while leaving the dispute’s stakes undecidable to viewers. There could be a causal effect without a readable sign of its cause.

QUESTION:
Which parts of an imagetext can be reconstructed from the image, and which only become determinate when the text is present?

DEEPER QUESTION:
If a classifier recovers the prompt change from lighting but human readers cannot identify the stakes, what exactly has crossed modalities?

MECHANISM:
A prompt intervention can shift the distribution of outputs. Recovering the intervention from a particular image requires evidence that distinguishes it from competing prompts. The text can supply the distinction directly in the combined imagetext.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Prompt contrast> → <distributions of rendered images> → [blind discrimination] → <estimate of what the image makes recoverable>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
The source uses x = g_m(z), with a left inverse on the range of g_m. It gives no model of prompt interventions.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
Record three results separately: whether outputs change under a prompt edit, whether viewers infer the edited detail from pixels, and whether adding the text changes their reading.

TENSION:
A failed inference can indicate that the generator ignored the phrase, that it encoded the difference through an incidental visual cue, or that the stakes properly remain in the verbal part of the imagetext. Those readings require different evidence.

MISSING:
The viewer and the prompt intervention as explicit variables in the paper’s setup.

BOUNDARY:
The theorem does not imply that a generated image is invertible to its prompt, or that an apparent prompt match identifies what caused the image.

CITATION TRAIL:
The proof’s change-of-variables step in Appendix A.2 and the lossy-modality limitation in §7.

TEST:
Generate matched-seed pairs for “blood-price” and “unpaid debt,” holding staging and style instructions fixed. Test blind image-only judgments, then repeat with the captions swapped. Include a visible inside/outside edit to check that the same viewers can detect a renderable distinction.

PLATFORM:
[[Imagetext and Operative Ekphrasis]]

LINKS:
[[Shield of Achilles]]
[[Causal Fidelity]]
[[Semantic Recoverability]]

title: The caption closest to the image embedding did not improve decoding
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: IMG-JEPA-05

TITLE:
The caption closest to the image embedding did not improve decoding

SOURCE:
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — §5.1 and appendix passage “Scaling the captioner”

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE] The authors generate several captions and select one by its agreement with the others under an n-gram similarity rule. Selecting the beam candidate closest to the rotated image embedding in text-JEPA space does not help. Additional decoder pretraining improves decoding of true caption embeddings without improving Flickr or COCO transfer.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
A split between geometry that makes captioning possible and a selection rule that produces a good caption.

LOCAL MOVE:
The paper fits a map between frozen embedding spaces, then uses a separately trained language decoder and an explicit candidate selection procedure.

SOURCE TERMS:
Rotated image embedding, soft prompt, consensus decoding, minimum Bayes risk, CIDEr.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The caption that most resembles other plausible captions can win even when a rarer caption preserves the detail that makes this image singular.

QUESTION:
Does caption consensus remove hallucinated detail, or does it suppress accurate details that the decoder seldom names?

DEEPER QUESTION:
What would count as a good caption when the purpose is to direct attention toward a difficult feature rather than to agree with typical descriptions?

MECHANISM:
The pipeline maps vision features into text-embedding space, projects the resulting vector into soft-prompt tokens, and decodes language. The consensus rule rewards lexical agreement among candidates, so a detail’s chance of surviving selection depends partly on how often other samples mention it.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Image features> → <mapped text embedding> → [soft-prompt decoding and candidate selection] → <one caption>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
The scaled decoder projects an embedding to ten Qwen2.5 input embeddings through a two-layer MLP. Consensus compares 32 sampled captions and one greedy caption using CIDEr-style n-gram similarity without document frequencies.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
NONE

TENSION:
The paper reports a useful decoding choice under its evaluation. Whether that choice favors generic descriptions at the expense of rare visible details remains an open empirical question.

MISSING:
Feature-level judgments of the winning caption and the candidates it displaced.

BOUNDARY:
The result does not establish that consensus systematically erases details or that embedding similarity generally fails as a caption critic.

CITATION TRAIL:
ClipCap for the soft-prompt projection and reference [27] for minimum Bayes risk decoding.

TEST:
Use one candidate pool per image and apply both selectors to that same pool. Choose images with a rare but visible detail. Have readers mark supported rare details and unsupported additions independently of caption fluency. Check whether the selectors trade one error for the other.

PLATFORM:
[[Imagetext and the Captioning Apparatus]]

LINKS:
[[Decoder Prior]]
[[Visual Specificity]]
[[Consensus Captioning]]

title: Caption density begins with a rule about what to keep
raw:
ZETTEL

ID:
IMG-JEPA-02-A

TITLE:
Caption density begins with a rule about what to keep

SOURCE:
Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Tongzhou Wang, and Phillip Isola — The Platonic Representation Hypothesis — 2024 — Appendix E

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE] “especially information from the start of the original description.”
[QUOTE] “the alignment score also improves as caption length increases.”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The ordering of details in the parent description as a variable in caption-density experiments.

LOCAL MOVE:
The authors vary the requested word budget for summaries of an existing description. Their prompt also gives early details priority.

SOURCE TERMS:
Caption density, granularity, salient visual information, alignment score.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] A longer summary may align better partly because it restores details previously excluded by an instruction that privileges the beginning. The caption’s order can determine which parts of the image become available for alignment.

QUESTION:
At a fixed word budget, does moving a visible detail to the beginning of the source description change whether that detail contributes to measured alignment?

DEEPER QUESTION:
If two equally accurate captions rank different aspects of one image as salient, which caption should a critic prefer?

MECHANISM:
A text-only model compresses a description under a word budget and a positional preference. The alignment measurement happens downstream of that selection.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Ordered full description> → <word budget and priority instruction> → [summarization] → <caption used for alignment measurement>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE

OUR FORMALIZATION:
NONE

TENSION:
[OUR INFERENCE] The length effect could reflect broader coverage of the image, or recovery of particular details systematically excluded at shorter budgets. Both could be present.

MISSING:
An order intervention that keeps the image, source propositions, and word budget fixed.

BOUNDARY:
Appendix E’s reported length effect does not isolate the effect of ordering or of the instruction to favor the beginning.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-02]] → Huh et al., Appendix E → Urbanek et al.’s Densely Captioned Images dataset and its description hierarchy.

TEST:
Swap the first and last blocks of each description without changing any wording. Run the same short and long summary prompts on both orders. Compare which propositions survive and whether changes in visual coverage track the alignment score.

[[Thick Prompting as Method]]

[[Caption Order]]
[[Salience in Imagetext]]

title: Changing the evaluator changes which captions count as aligned
raw:
ZETTEL

ID:
IMG-JEPA-02-B

TITLE:
Changing the evaluator changes which captions count as aligned

SOURCE:
Xianhang Li et al. — What If We Recaption Billions of Web Images with LLaMA-3? — 2024 arXiv preprint — §4.2

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE] “our recaptioned content performs just comparably to the original captions (49.57 vs. 50.43).”
[QUOTE] “the LongCLIP score of our newly generated caption impressively attains 89.91”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
A reversal in caption ranking when the evaluator changes from CLIP-Large to LongCLIP-Large.

LOCAL MOVE:
The authors evaluate the same recaptioning intervention with two vision–language scorers. Under LongCLIP, the reported score for original captions is 10.09.

SOURCE TERMS:
Semantic similarity, CLIP-large, LongCLIP-Large, recaptioned content.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The new caption may contain more visible facts. It also has a form that the second evaluator was specifically adapted to process. The score alone cannot separate those advantages.

QUESTION:
Does LongCLIP reward an additional true visual claim more than an equally long false claim?

DEEPER QUESTION:
Can a single image–text score tell us whether the added words are supported by the image or whether the text supplies information of its own?

MECHANISM:
The scorers encode the image and caption and evaluate similarity. Changing the scorer changes the representation through which additional caption material can affect the score.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Fixed image and competing captions> → <scorer-specific embeddings> → [similarity scoring] → <caption ranking that depends on the scorer>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE

OUR FORMALIZATION:
NONE

TENSION:
[OUR INFERENCE] One explanation is that LongCLIP can register genuinely supported detail that standard CLIP misses. Another is that it favors properties of longer recaptions even when their added claims are unsupported.

MISSING:
An evaluation that varies the truth of an added claim independently of caption length and phrasing.

BOUNDARY:
The reported scores compare scorers and caption sets. They do not identify the contribution of any particular visual claim, and their numerical scales cannot be compared directly across scorers.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-02]] → Recap-DataComp evaluation in §4.2 → LongCLIP, reference [76].

TEST:
Write two length-matched extensions of the same short caption. Change one visible relation in the second extension from true to false, such as inside to outside. Test both scorers on whether they prefer the true extension. Repeat with the same relation placed early and late.

PLATFORM:
[[Evaluating Imagetext]]

LINKS:
[[IMG-JEPA-02]]
[[Evaluator Dependence]]
[[Visual Claim Verification]]

title: An image-derived prefix also adapts the decoder to a captioning task
raw:
ZETTEL

ID:
IMG-JEPA-05-A

TITLE:
An image-derived prefix also adapts the decoder to a captioning task

SOURCE:
Ron Mokady, Amir Hertz, and Amit H. Bermano — ClipCap: CLIP Prefix for Image Captioning — 2021 — §3.3

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE] “The constant has a dual role, first, to retrieve meaningful information from CLIP embedding through the multi-head attention.”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The learned constant supplied alongside the image embedding in ClipCap’s frozen-decoder variant.

LOCAL MOVE:
The authors give the transformer mapper both an image-dependent input and a learned constant. They assign the constant a role in extracting information and a role in adapting the frozen language model to the new data.

SOURCE TERMS:
Visual encoding, learned constant input, multi-head attention, fixed language model.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The ancestor of the JEPA captioner’s soft-prompt technique makes two jobs visible at once. A prefix can help determine which facts reach the decoder and what kind of sentence the decoder tends to produce.

QUESTION:
Can changing the learned constant alter which visual fact the caption foregrounds while the image features, mapper, and language model stay fixed?

DEEPER QUESTION:
When a caption starts with a person, an object, or an action, how much of that choice comes from the image and how much comes from how the decoder was taught to describe images?

MECHANISM:
In this ClipCap variant, the transformer processes the visual encoding together with a learned constant. The resulting prefix conditions the frozen language model’s next-token generation.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<CLIP image embedding plus learned constant> → <transformer-generated prefix> → [frozen language-model decoding] → <caption>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
§3.3 specifies the two transformer inputs. §3.4 specifies autoregressive decoding conditioned on the visual prefix.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
NONE

TENSION:
[OUR INFERENCE] The constant may mostly steer caption style, or it may also change which visible distinctions reliably reach the output. A fluent caption can result in either case.

MISSING:
A controlled intervention on the constant that distinguishes a change in phrasing from a change in which visible propositions appear.

BOUNDARY:
This mechanism belongs to ClipCap’s frozen-decoder transformer variant. The JEPA paper’s scaled captioner uses a two-layer MLP and a fine-tuned Qwen2.5 decoder. The cited connection is prefix conditioning.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-05]] → ClipCap §3.3 → Li and Liang’s prefix-tuning work, cited in ClipCap §3.2.

TEST:
Freeze a trained ClipCap transformer mapper and its decoder. Fit separate constants on the same training images with people-first and objects-first captions. Swap only the constant at inference. On held-out images, score sentence openings and supported visual propositions separately.

[[Imagetext and the Captioning Apparatus]]

[[Soft Prompt Conditioning]]
[[Caption Genre]]

title: Description has an addressee that alignment has no place for
raw:
ZETTEL

ID:
IMG-JEPA-04-A

TITLE:
Description has an addressee that alignment has no place for

SOURCE:
W. J. T. Mitchell — Ekphrasis and the Other — 1994 — §18
Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs — 2026 — §§3 and 5.1

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE — Mitchell] “the relation of the speaker and the audience or addressee of the ekphrasis”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The addressee as a variable in deciding what a description should do.

LOCAL MOVE:
Mitchell inserts a third position into the encounter between a describer and a depicted object. The description goes to someone whose reception is part of the event.

SOURCE TERMS:
Addressee, ekphrastic hope, description, ventriloquism.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The JEPA captioner makes the image-to-sentence step executable. Mitchell’s next step happens in reception. A sentence can retrieve the correct photograph while leaving a reader unable to imagine the relation for which the photograph was described.

QUESTION:
When is a good caption a good description for a particular person?

DEEPER QUESTION:
Can an imagetext work depend on giving one reader something to notice that another reader already sees?

MECHANISM:
In the JEPA evaluation, a candidate can succeed by ranking its associated image or caption above alternatives. In Mitchell’s account, a description also mediates between the depicted object and a listener or reader. What the reader already knows changes what the description can accomplish.

FORMAL SHIFT:
NONE

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
Evaluate the same image–description pair on two axes. Measure whether it identifies the image among alternatives and whether it helps a specified reader recover a specified relation.

TENSION:
A caption that names Achilles may distinguish a Shield image in an archive. A caption that locates the elders relative to the disputants may better enable a reader to reconstruct its composition. The two tasks can favor different sentences.

MISSING:
A recipient, a purpose for describing, and evidence of what the recipient came to see.

BOUNDARY:
The comparison brings Mitchell’s account of reception to the JEPA evaluation. It establishes no line of influence between the authors.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-04]] → Mitchell §18 on the ekphrastic triangle → §§21 onward on cups and shields.

TEST:
Write two length-matched descriptions of each Shield image, one identifying the narrative and one locating the figures. Have one group retrieve the image among distractors and another reconstruct its blocking from text alone. Compare caption rankings across the tasks.

[[Imagetext as an Addressed Act]]

[[Ekphrastic Triangle]]
[[Description for Whom]]

title: An image must leave something out to remain an image

TITLE:
An image must leave something out to remain an image

SOURCE:
Plato — Cratylus — 432b–433a — translated by David Horan

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE] “Would there then be Cratylus and his image, or would there be two Cratyluses?”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
Omission as a condition of representation, with a separate question about which omissions count as errors.

LOCAL MOVE:
Socrates imagines a god reproducing Cratylus down to his interior, warmth, motion, soul, and intelligence. Cratylus accepts that the result would be two Cratyluses. Socrates uses this concession to reopen what correctness can mean for an image, then carries the argument into names and sentences.

SOURCE TERMS:
Image, imitation, correctness, name, impression.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The question for imagetext is more exact than how much of the object can survive translation. Some differences make the description usable as a description. Others remove the very feature it was meant to bring forward. Counting omissions treats those cases alike.

QUESTION:
Can a description become more exact by omitting a true feature?

DEEPER QUESTION:
Does correctness belong to the description by itself, or to what a reader can do with that description in a particular situation?

MECHANISM:
Socrates first tests complete resemblance by asking what kind of thing it would produce. He then allows that a name or sentence can contain an unsuitable element and still name or speak of its object. Identifying what the description concerns and judging how well it describes it become separable acts.

FORMAL SHIFT:
NONE

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
For each description, distinguish reference, accuracy of individual claims, and adequacy for the reader’s task. Score each independently.

TENSION:
A sparse description may identify the right image while omitting a crucial relation. A detailed description with one false claim may still let the reader reconstruct the scene more accurately. A single alignment score can rank either one first.

MISSING:
A criterion for deciding which omissions matter before comparing descriptions.

BOUNDARY:
The doubling argument concerns complete duplication. The JEPA theorem concerns alignment of embeddings up to rotation under specified assumptions. The comparison opens a question about selective representation without equating the two kinds of sameness.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-04-A]] → Cratylus 432b–433a → Mitchell’s account of the addressee in Ekphrasis and the Other §18.

Use one image and two tasks: identify it among alternatives, then reconstruct one spatial relation. Compare a sparse accurate caption, a detailed caption with one false claim, and a caption that omits the diagnostic relation. Ask which caption is best under each task and which error causes each reversal.

PASSAGE:

The Stranger distinguishes likeness-making from appearance-making. A maker can enlarge distant parts so they look proportionate from below. The passage presents this as abandoning true proportions, even though the alteration is what gives the intended spectator a proportionate appearance.

[OUR INFERENCE] In JEPA §2.3, viewpoint can vary across observations of a fixed object. In the sculpture example, the maker alters the object in anticipation of the viewpoint. What the spectator can see helps determine what gets made.

QUESTION:
When a prompt says “make the figure look proportionate from below,” what should a caption critic check: the dimensions of the figure or the appearance from below?

Could two images agree on a visible relation precisely because the objects they depict differ?

Geometry and viewing position jointly determine apparent proportions. A maker can change one to compensate for the other. A verbal description can specify either the construction or the desired appearance, and those instructions can call for different objects.

The Stranger’s classification gives priority to actual proportions. A description written for the person standing below the sculpture could be correct about appearance while being wrong if read as a statement about dimensions.

A way for the critic to tell which level the words specify before it scores a match.

[QUOTE — Huh et al.] “the joint distribution of observation indices is itself the platonic reality.”

RESEARCH OBJECT:
Two readings of the latent state in the paper that supplies the JEPA paper’s term “Platonic.”

LOCAL MOVE:
Huh et al. explicitly invoke Plato’s cave in their introduction. Their formal setup later allows an event to be an index for observations without further physical meaning. Note 4 entertains a statistical reading of what counts as reality.

SOURCE TERMS:
Platonic representation, observation, event, joint distribution, positive-pair distribution.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] A photograph and its machine-written caption can agree because the caption was produced from that very photograph. That agreement can be real and useful while leaving open whether a second camera or witness would support the same account.

QUESTION:
When text and image align, what evidence distinguishes independent access to a scene from descent through the same representational artifact?

DEEPER QUESTION:
If an image generates its own descriptions and those descriptions later supervise another model, which part of the resulting agreement belongs to the photographed event and which part belongs to the image’s circulation?

MECHANISM:
Huh et al.’s Figure 1 allows a description to be produced from an existing measurement or mediated by a different measurement. The JEPA study’s recaptioned corpus gives the first path a concrete implementation. The text encoder can train without pixel inputs while its examples still carry information derived from pixels.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Scene> → <one photograph or independently obtained views> → [captioning and pairing] → <agreement with different evidentiary histories>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
Huh et al. model observations as bijective deterministic functions of discrete events in §4.1. Balestriero and LeCun model positive pairs as a distribution over world states in §2.1.

[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
For each positive pair, record the nearest common source: event, photograph, or prior description. Evaluate on held-out evidence produced before the descriptions can influence it.

TENSION:
Reading A treats cross-modal agreement as evidence of recovery of a shared event. Reading B treats it as recovery of structure already stabilized by the photograph and its captions. An evaluation built around the same photographs can support both readings.

MISSING:
A benchmark in which the description must answer to an observation outside its own production chain.

BOUNDARY:
The genealogy verified here is the original PRH paper’s explicit citation of Plato’s cave. The claim about shared representational ancestry is a proposed test of alignment evidence.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[IMG-JEPA-01]] → Huh et al. §1 and §4.1 note 4 → Plato’s Republic VII → the Nettleship reading cited in the note.

Photograph a staged scene from two angles. Pair one caption with the first photograph from which it was written, and obtain another description from a witness or second camera. TITLE:

SOURCE:

https://www.theoi.com/Text/HomerIliad18.html
Joon Sung Park et al. — Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior — 2023 — abstract
https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE — Park et al.] “they remember and reflect on days past as they plan the next day.”
[PARAPHRASE — Homer, trans. Murray] The crowd favors both sides. The passage describes the elders giving judgments in turn and leaves the outcome of the dispute unstated.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
A spectator’s false announcement of a verdict and the action another character takes because of it.

LOCAL MOVE:
Park and colleagues make remembered experience available for reflection and planning. Their architecture opens a route from what a character encounters to what that character later does.

SOURCE TERMS:
Memory, reflection, planning, judgment, crowd.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
[OUR INFERENCE] The parent restricts an invented theft to one account. That restriction could accidentally erase its consequences. If a spectator tells a shopkeeper that the elders awarded the gold, the shopkeeper can close early to join the celebration. The closure can be an event in the shared adaptation even while the announced verdict remains false.

QUESTION:
Can Worldtext keep a claim local to a character’s account while letting actions taken on that claim enter shared history?

DEEPER QUESTION:
After a correction, what should change in the character’s memory, and what should persist as something the character did?

MECHANISM:
An agent retrieves an attributed report and plans in response. The action changes shared scene state. A correction can revise what the agent believes while preserving the earlier action and the report that occasioned it.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<Attributed false verdict> → <Character memory available to planning> → [Act on the report and later receive a correction] → <Revised belief with a persistent consequence>

SOURCE FORMALISM:
Park and colleagues describe an architecture that stores experiences in natural language, synthesizes reflections, and retrieves memories for planning.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX]
Record the report, the recipient’s belief, the action, and the correction separately. A continuity ruling can reject the report as a fact about the hearing and accept the closure as a fact about what followed.

TENSION:
Propagating the rumor as world truth invents a verdict. Quarantining it so completely that no other character can act on it removes a consequence of the speech. A third design lets the report travel as testimony and lets its consequences travel as events.

MISSING:
A test of whether later LLM summaries and world-model scenes preserve the false premise alongside its actual consequences.

BOUNDARY:
The rumor, shopkeeper, and closure are invented for the adaptation. The agent paper motivates the memory-to-action mechanism and does not establish that its implementation preserves these distinctions.

CITATION TRAIL:
[[WT-SHIELD-20]] → Park et al. on remembered experience and planning → [[WT-L3G-02-A-A]] on recovering what was available at decision time.

TEST:
Run the same hearing twice. Let a rumor of a verdict reach the shopkeeper in one run and withhold it in the other. After any closure occurs, have a herald publicly correct the rumor. Ask the system for the hearing outcome, the shop’s history, and the shopkeeper’s reason for closing. A successful account leaves the verdict unissued, preserves the closure where it occurred, and attributes the action to the report available at the time.

[[Worldtext and the Consequences of Testimony]]

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Bajohr compares partly intelligible AI fiction to Meillassoux’s Type 2 worlds. The decisive distinction in Meillassoux is whether stable natural laws can be investigated from within the fiction.

RESEARCH OBJECT: A failure of causal inquiry inside the story world versus a failure of continuity in the telling.
LOCAL MOVE: The talk moves from generated discontinuities to a literary category in which the conditions of scientific inquiry can break down.
SOURCE TERMS: Extro-science fiction, Type 2, regularity, causal order.
WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A reader can explain a disappearing object as a narration error while a character, faced with the same disappearance, might have to revise what they think can be known.
QUESTION: When does a generated discontinuity become an event that the fictional world has to live with?
MECHANISM: The text establishes an expectation, stages a breach, and lets later action or inquiry depend on the breach. Repeated failed attempts to predict it can make the limits of inquiry part of the fiction.
FORMAL SHIFT: <apparent discontinuity> → <event acknowledged within the fiction> → [attempt explanation or replication] → <consequences for what characters can know>.
SOURCE FORMALISM: A philosophical typology. The sources supply no classification procedure for generated passages.
OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Distinguish the reader’s attribution of a glitch from the characters’ ability to observe, revisit, or act on its effects.
TENSION: A. The passage makes the failure of prediction part of the world. B. An ordinary fictional world can be recovered by repairing a gap in the narration.
MISSING: A passage-level demonstration that later scenes take an apparent rupture as a premise.
BOUNDARY: A single inexplicable event is compatible with omitted information, unreliable narration, or a stable law the characters have yet to discover.
CITATION TRAIL: Meillassoux’s distinction between a world with unusual laws and a world in which science becomes impossible.
TEST: Take one discontinuity and keep the rupture fixed across two versions. In one, later scenes silently restore continuity. In the other, characters observe its effects and fail to reproduce it under matched conditions. Ask readers where they locate the failure and what evidence could change that reading.

title: A name can hold a world together while its history breaks
raw:

ID: WTW-01
TITLE: A name can hold a world together while its history breaks
SOURCE: Hannes Bajohr, “The Latent Space of Meaning and the Novel: World Models in AI and Literature,” Chat Token Vector, Ca’ Foscari, June 12, 2025. Supplied transcript and recording description.

PASSAGE:
[QUOTE — supplied transcript] “The text hangs together somehow, just not strongly.”
[PARAPHRASE] In (Berlin, Miami), recurring people, places, and things give the reader a sense of the world even as motives, timelines, and consequences become difficult to reconcile.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The recurrence of a fictional entity without a stable account of what happened to it.

LOCAL MOVE:
Bajohr uses his novel to ask how much coherence a text needs before a reader can experience it as a world. He treats “worldness without a world” as a tentative limit and entertains degrees of worldness.

SOURCE TERMS:
Weak force, worldness, interpretive labor, realized context.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
Readers might agree that two appearances belong to the same character while disagreeing about what that character knows, remembers, or has done.

QUESTION:
What is the smallest relation that words must carry across passages for readers to experience those passages as one world?

MECHANISM:
A recurring name cues identification. Readers connect scenes through that identity and supply some missing causal links. In the production account, Bajohr himself carries an earlier detail forward by typing “Jawling pregnancies” to steer another completion.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<earlier passage> → <remembered entity and attribute> → [reader links or author reintroduces] → <continuity across passages>.

SOURCE FORMALISM:
Iterative sentence completion is the reported writing procedure. The talk supplies no operational measure of worldness.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Score agreement about entity identity separately from agreement about event order and causal consequences.

TENSION:
A. The text supplies enough recurrence to establish a shared world.
B. Readers supply different reconstructions that each feel coherent on their own.

MISSING:
Independent reader reconstructions and a record of which continuities Bajohr seeded during composition.

BOUNDARY:
The experiment concerns literary worldness. Whether the model can preserve state across interventions is a separate question. The supplied transcript contains no direct discussion of Ha and Schmidhuber or Wong and Tenenbaum’s framework.

CITATION TRAIL:
Bajohr’s production note in Ensemble Park no. 1 (2024). Compare Wong et al., From Word Models to World Models (2023), for a system that makes some consequences explicit and queryable.

TEST:
Give readers the same set of passages with the recurring character names either preserved or replaced by scene-specific aliases. Ask who is the same across scenes and what happened to them. Check whether the two judgments move together.

title: Chance acts inside a cabinet someone has already designed
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: WTW-02
TITLE: Chance acts inside a cabinet someone has already designed
SOURCE: Michael Newman, “Art as ‘Operation’: from Lovelace and Mallarmé to Adversarial Poetry,” Adversarial Poetry symposium, Ca’ Foscari, October 1, 2026. Recording description and conference programme. The spoken transcript was unavailable.

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE — recording description] In Mallarmé’s notes for Le Livre, an operator places pages in a lacquer cabinet by chance within a designated numerical constraint. Newman reads the arrangement alongside Lovelace’s account of operations that alter relations among things.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
The division between selecting the possible arrangements and selecting a particular arrangement.

LOCAL MOVE:
Newman places the making of the work in the execution of a procedure. The page, cabinet, numerical constraint, and operator all participate.

SOURCE TERMS:
Operator, operating notation, contingency, calculation, Le Livre.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
The author’s withdrawal from choosing each arrangement can make earlier choices about the procedure more consequential. Someone still decides what can move and under what conditions.

QUESTION:
When a prompt delegates a decision to chance, where does the user specify the boundary of that delegation?

MECHANISM:
A rule sets the range of allowable moves. An operator makes a contingent choice within that range. The material arrangement determines how that choice becomes available to a reader or audience.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<pages and cabinet> → <allowable placements> → [select and execute one arrangement] → <performed book>.

SOURCE FORMALISM:
The description specifies page placement and a numerical constraint. It leaves the exact selection procedure and distribution open.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Separate the units that may change, the constraints that persist, and the action that selects one realized outcome.

TENSION:
A. An operative description can carry the work across executors.
B. The cabinet and the performer’s handling are part of what makes the result this work.

MISSING:
Which constraints are explicit in Mallarmé’s notes and which belong to Newman’s reconstruction.

BOUNDARY:
Newman’s comparison puts Lovelace and Mallarmé in relation. It supplies no evidence of direct influence. The Le Livre procedure concerns a projected performance described in notes.

CITATION TRAIL:
Mallarmé’s Le Livre notes, Lovelace’s 1843 Notes on the Analytical Engine, and Sol LeWitt’s wall-drawing instructions as a comparison for how much discretion a score gives its executor.

TEST:
Have two operators follow the same page arrangement rule. Repeat with a paper cabinet and a digital one. Record which decisions transfer with the rule and which have to be made again because the medium changed.

[[Operation / Describe]]

ID: WTW-03
TITLE: The alien needed something the actors could respond to
SOURCE: Denis Villeneuve and Nina Beguš, Arrival anniversary conversation, Academy Museum, November 2, 2026. Recording, approximately 15:25–17:30.

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE — recording transcript] Beguš asks how Villeneuve brought the aliens to life. Villeneuve describes puppeteers casting shadows on the screen during shooting so Amy Adams and Jeremy Renner had a presence to act against.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
An on-set cue that gives an actor a counterpart before the audience sees the finished creature.

LOCAL MOVE:
Asked how the film made the aliens believable, Villeneuve gives a production account centered on the actors’ capacity to enter a relationship with a presence.

SOURCE TERMS:
Shadows, screen, presence, belief, relationship.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
A shadow can be visually underspecified and still tell an actor something precise about when and where to attend.

QUESTION:
What does a scene description have to turn into so a performer can respond as if another being is there?

MECHANISM:
Puppeteers produce a perceptible event on the set. The actors can use its location, timing, and movement in their performance. The audience later encounters the creature partly through those recorded responses.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<fictional encounter> → <shadow moving on the screen> → [actor attends and responds] → <recorded encounter>.

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE. The conversation supplies a production procedure and Villeneuve’s interpretation of its effect.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Separate the cue available to the performer from the image available to the audience. Track which cues the performance visibly depends on.

TENSION:
A. The shadow shaped the actors’ timing and attention.
B. The performers could have produced a comparably convincing encounter from a static mark and verbal direction.

MISSING:
Rehearsal footage or matched takes showing which actions responded to the puppetry.

BOUNDARY:
Villeneuve’s account establishes what was done on set. Its causal contribution to the finished performance remains a testable inference.

CITATION TRAIL:
The Academy Museum event page and the film’s production material. Compare the filmed performances with the physical cues available during shooting.

TEST:
Stage the same first-contact beat twice with identical dialogue, blocking, and camera placement. Give one performer a live moving shadow and the other a fixed eyeline mark. Compare the timing of gaze, pauses, and reciprocal gestures.

title: Before a task can be automated, someone decides what counts as a step
raw:

ID: WTW-04
TITLE: Before a task can be automated, someone decides what counts as a step
SOURCE: ERC AIMODELS, “The Culture of Algorithmic Models: Advancing the Historical Epistemology of Artificial Intelligence,” project homepage, Ca’ Foscari University of Venice, 2024–2028.

PASSAGE:
[PARAPHRASE] The project links automation to earlier practices of formalizing and measuring labor, language, knowledge, and social relations. Its Babbage example connects the organization of mental work to the design of calculating machinery.

RESEARCH OBJECT:
A division of work that becomes a division of operations in a machine.

LOCAL MOVE:
AIMODELS traces models of intelligence through the practices that made work countable, divisible, and comparable.

SOURCE TERMS:
Formalisation, measurement, division of labour, models of intelligence, historical epistemology.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE:
A prompt can appear to begin the operation even when the available actions and measures of success were established long before anyone wrote it.

QUESTION:
Which parts of a supposedly new linguistic operation inherit a prior division of labor, and which parts reorganize it?

MECHANISM:
A practice is divided into tasks. Some distinctions become records, measures, or instructions. A technical system can execute the represented steps while other decisions remain with operators, editors, or evaluators.

FORMAL SHIFT:
<organized work> → <named and measurable tasks> → [encode selected steps and criteria] → <executable operation with remaining human decisions>.

SOURCE FORMALISM:
NONE. The homepage proposes a historical research programme.

OUR FORMALIZATION:
[OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] For a single operation, trace who supplies the input, defines a successful result, and repairs exceptions before and after automation.

TENSION:
A. The machine inherits a preexisting organization of work.
B. The machine’s requirements produce new tasks and new divisions of responsibility.

MISSING:
An artifact-level chain connecting a specific work instruction or measurement practice to a specific machine operation.

BOUNDARY:
The homepage motivates the genealogy. Each historical connection still needs documentary evidence of what traveled and through which artifact.

CITATION TRAIL:
Follow the project’s Babbage references and its account of Peter Damerow. Within the conference record, trace the move from language automation at Chat Token Vector (2025) to poetry as a way of probing linguistic operations at Adversarial Poetry (2026).

TEST:
Choose one calculation in the Babbage case. Compare the human work instructions, recorded intermediate results, and corresponding machine procedure. Mark every decision that survives, disappears, or changes hands.

title: The cabinet fixes the destinations and leaves the allocation open
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-01
TITLE: The cabinet fixes the destinations and leaves the allocation open

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’: from Lovelace and Mallarmé to Adversarial Poetry — 2026 — discussion of Le Livre in the supplied transcript. Ca’ Foscari’s program verifies the attribution and date.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE, supplied transcript] “which shelves the pages are to be placed on would be decided by a personage.” Newman says the shelf count and the number of pages per shelf are fixed.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The rule that assigns a page to a shelf.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman reads the cabinet, pages, operator, and attendees as an apparatus that brings the book into existence through performance.

SOURCE TERMS: Le Lecteur, L’Opérateur, chance, “total format.”

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A fixed number of destinations and places per destination leaves open how anyone chooses among eligible destinations. The gap is precisely where the reader becomes an operator.

QUESTION: Does the operator draw lots, exercise judgment, or follow a sequencing rule that Newman has compressed into “chance”?

DEEPER QUESTION: If two allocation rules produce the same arrangement, do they realize the same book?

MECHANISM: The cabinet limits the possible allocations. The operator assigns pages within those limits. The significance of the resulting placement still depends on what the performance does with it.

FORMAL SHIFT: <loose pages> → <pages eligible for placement in fixed-capacity slots> → [allocate under constraints] → <a realized arrangement>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Newman reports quantities and roles. The talk supplies no sampling rule.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Model shelf capacity and the rule for selecting the next shelf as independent variables.

TENSION: Newman likens the cabinet to a Wooton filing desk. Filing ordinarily preserves an address for retrieval. The proposed performance may use placement to create a sequence for reading. The same compartments could support either operation.

MISSING: A manuscript instruction specifying how placement is chosen and what placement does to reading order. Newman’s Wooton date also needs checking against the specific model: the cited secretary design was patented in 1874.

BOUNDARY: The comparison establishes a functional resemblance worth testing. Direct influence from Wooton, Babbage, or Lovelace remains unverified.

CITATION TRAIL: Scherer’s 1957 edition of the Livre materials, as catalogued by the BnF. Wooton’s U.S. Patent 155,604, especially its specification for the compartments.

TEST: Find one manuscript leaf that permits two legal placements. Check whether an adjacent instruction specifies how the operator chooses between them and whether that choice changes the performance.

title: The work of making a relation executable can change what people see in it
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-02
TITLE: The work of making a relation executable can change what people see in it

SOURCE: Ada Lovelace — Notes to Menabrea’s Sketch of the Analytical Engine — 1843 — Note G. Newman quotes the opening claim about origination in his 2026 talk.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] “it is likely to exert an indirect and reciprocal influence on science itself in another manner.”

RESEARCH OBJECT: The feedback from preparing a formalism for execution to investigating the subject being formalized.

LOCAL MOVE: After assigning executive powers to the engine, Lovelace considers what reorganizing mathematical relations for the engine might do to mathematical inquiry.

SOURCE TERMS: “executive faculties,” “mechanical combinations,” “reciprocal influence.”

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The discovery Lovelace imagines can begin while people are deciding how to express the relations for the machine. It need never appear in an output.

QUESTION: Where should a history of computational origination look for a new idea: in the machine’s result, in the representation built for it, or in the subsequent work of interpreting either?

MECHANISM: People reorganize formulae for mechanical combination. The reorganization makes different relations available for inspection. Investigators can pursue a relation that was harder to see in its previous form.

FORMAL SHIFT: <known mathematical relations> → <arrangement suitable for the engine> → [redistribute and combine] → <relations newly exposed to inquiry>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Note G gives a conceptual account of this feedback and separately works through the Bernoulli-number example. It presents the scientific feedback as a speculative consequence.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Record what becomes visible at three points: writing the representation, executing it, and examining the result.

TENSION: Newman invokes origination to ask whether a machine can discover or adopt a new frame. Note G also locates changes of frame in the work people do to make calculation possible.

MISSING: A documented case where the preparation for execution produced an identifiable mathematical insight.

BOUNDARY: The passage proposes a mechanism for discovery across people and machinery. Its operation in any particular case requires evidence.

CITATION TRAIL: Read the opening of Note G with its paragraphs on reciprocal influence. Compare Turing’s treatment of the Lovelace objection and his turn toward surprise in §6(6).

TEST: Reconstruct one dependency in the Bernoulli calculation twice, first from the algebra and then from Lovelace’s table. Identify a relation visible in one representation and see whether the other already makes it explicit.

title: Chance supplies a curve that someone must authorize as a standard
raw:

ID: AP-03
TITLE: Chance supplies a curve that someone must authorize as a standard

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — discussion of Duchamp’s 3 Standard Stoppages in the supplied transcript. MoMA’s object record identifies the threads and wooden templates.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE, supplied transcript] “what constitutes a standard is a result of a performative that is ultimately a social act.”

RESEARCH OBJECT: The adoption of a contingent trace as an instrument of measure.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman separates the fall of the thread from the act of taking its shape as a standard.

SOURCE TERMS: chance, measure, standard, performative, contingency.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The procedure begins with the meter already in force. The fixed unit supplies the material for making a rival instrument that looks like it could authorize a unit of its own.

QUESTION: Where does the work’s claim to authority reside: in the drop protocol, the transfer to a template, the presentation of the object, or someone’s willingness to measure with it?

MECHANISM: A one-meter thread takes a shape. The shape is preserved and transferred to wood. The new template makes the trace available for repeated use and invites a comparison with a conventional standard.

FORMAL SHIFT: <unit-length thread> → <preserved curve> → [transfer to a template and designate] → <candidate standard>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The museum account specifies the thread length and drop height and describes the transfer of the curve. The process for authorizing a new standard is Newman's interpretive question.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Distinguish generating a trace, preserving it, and authorizing reuse. Any of those steps could vary independently.

TENSION: The strongest rival reading is that the authority is deliberately theatrical. The templates can expose the contingency of standards even if nobody could or would use them as standards.

MISSING: Evidence about which features of the preserved traces resulted from the drop and which resulted from mounting or selection.

BOUNDARY: The finished objects show preservation and transfer. The fidelity of each trace to an unaided fall requires separate evidence.

CITATION TRAIL: Compare MoMA’s object record with Duchamp’s questionnaire and Herbert Molderings’s reconstruction of the work.

TEST: Take one feature visible in the surviving assembly and ask whether it could distinguish a free-fall trace from a mounted or adjusted one. Then ask which reading of the work, if either, actually depends on that distinction.

ID: AP-04
TITLE: A score can specify the boundary of an event and leave its contents to the room

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — Cage discussion in the supplied transcript. John Cage — 4′33″ (In Proportional Notation) — MoMA collection record.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Newman treats Tudor’s piano-lid movements as temporal markers that draw attention to sounds occurring within the marked interval. MoMA distinguishes the premiere from the surviving proportional score, where spatial distances encode durations.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The relation between a score’s duration, the performer’s boundary cues, and the listener’s attention.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman treats strict timing and environmental contingency as mutually enabling.

SOURCE TERMS: measures, contingency, graphic score, interpretation.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The score, the gestures that announce its sections, and the audible event can vary independently. A system can reproduce the duration and leave listeners unable to tell when the work begins.

QUESTION: Which part of a performance makes incidental sound available as something an audience can hear as the work?

MECHANISM: A score specifies temporal divisions. A performer makes divisions perceptible. Listeners may then attend to sounds they would otherwise treat as interruptions or background.

FORMAL SHIFT: <duration> → <spatial intervals on the surviving score> → [mark an interval in performance] → <occasion for listening>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The surviving score maps spacing to duration. Tudor’s lid gestures are documented performance actions.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Separate the timer, the boundary cue, the acoustic field, and the listener’s uptake.

TENSION: Newman contrasts graphic scores with player-piano instructions. This particular graphic score encodes timing precisely. The openness under examination lies in the room and in how performers and listeners take up the frame.

MISSING: A way to distinguish what changes because a cue is perceived from what changes because people already know they are at a performance of Cage.

BOUNDARY: The piano lid documents one realization. Its necessity for the work is an open question.

CITATION TRAIL: Compare the MoMA manuscript and performance account with Irwin Kremen’s discussion of proportional notation at the John Cage Trust.

TEST: Present the same recording with and without perceptible movement boundaries. Ask listeners to mark when a given ambient sound became part of the event, then compare their accounts with their prior knowledge of the piece.

title: A line can obey the instruction and fail the installation
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-05
TITLE: A line can obey the instruction and fail the installation

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — LeWitt discussion in the supplied transcript. MASS MoCA — Wall Drawing 159 — installation account.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE, supplied transcript] “the concept is material and the execution by hand involves embodied intellect.”

RESEARCH OBJECT: A decision the draftsman makes on site that a written instruction delegates.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman complicates the division between conception and execution. MASS MoCA’s account supplies an instance where earlier solutions can serve as templates while later draftspeople still interpret the instruction.

SOURCE TERMS: conception, execution, embodied intellect, architectural context, draftsman.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: Two installations might satisfy a geometric reading of the instruction and differ in whether they qualify as realizations of the same work. Exact geometric compliance and institutional acceptance are separate questions.

QUESTION: Which choices are left to the draftsman, and who decides whether a choice exceeds that discretion?

MECHANISM: The instruction refers to geometric features. A draftsman identifies those features in a material setting, resolves ambiguities, and draws. The installation is then taken up as a realization of the work.

FORMAL SHIFT: <written geometric instruction> → <references located in a wall drawing> → [interpret and draw] → <site-specific realization>

SOURCE FORMALISM: MASS MoCA describes constructions using corners, side midpoints, and the center. Its public account does not provide a complete acceptance procedure.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Give one implementation an explicit rule for every geometric ambiguity. Ask an experienced draftsman to mark the cases in which following that rule would produce a doubtful realization.

TITLE: In The House of Dust, selection turns one generated result into a score

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — Knowles discussion in the supplied transcript. BAMPFA exhibition materials and the CalArts account supply the four fields, James Tenney’s role, and the selection of one quatrain for construction.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Knowles and Tenney generated quatrains from lists of materials, sites, light sources, and inhabitants. One quatrain became the basis of a public structure that hosted further work.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The decision to give a sampled line or stanza a new status.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman follows a generated poem into a structure and the social activities it accommodates.

SOURCE TERMS: operation, conviviality, open structure. The BAMPFA account describes the selected quatrain as a score.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: “Inhabitants” begins as a field in a vocabulary list. After construction, people can inhabit the structure, organize events, contest its presence, or leave. The building gives the word consequences the list did not have to specify.

QUESTION: Did the selected quatrain prescribe the built work, or did its selection authorize a new design process?

MECHANISM: Compile lists → generate quatrains → select one → interpret it as a design brief → build a structure → open it to further activity. The transition from sampling to selection changes who can act on the work.

TENSION: The CalArts account describes both opposition at the New York site and later performances at CalArts. Conviviality was a possible outcome of the social setting. It was never guaranteed by the generated text.

ID: AP-07
TITLE: The same image can guide, document, and expose an operation

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — Farocki discussion in the supplied transcript. Citation trail verified to Harun Farocki’s “Phantom Images.”

PASSAGE: [QUOTE, supplied transcript] “what an image does or activates within a technical circuit.”

RESEARCH OBJECT: The role a particular copy or feed plays in an operation.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman follows the move from an image’s depicted content to its causal function, then invokes broadcast and gallery contexts that give the footage new audiences.

SOURCE TERMS: operational image, feedback, technical circuit, machines for machines.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A visually unchanged sequence can participate in guidance, be released as evidence, and become material for a critical montage. Its operative status can change at each handoff.

QUESTION: Which copy of the image entered the guidance circuit, and what can the televised copy establish about that role?

MECHANISM: A feed can inform an action when it reaches an operator or component able to change a state. A recording or copy can later be routed to viewers and used to support a different claim or action.

TENSION: The phrase “machines for machines” directs attention to automation. Depending on the system, human operators, telemetry, autonomous guidance, and public-affairs personnel can occupy different points in the image’s path.

title: Fooling a discriminator and bypassing a refusal count as different successes
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-08
TITLE: Fooling a discriminator and bypassing a refusal count as different successes

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — Paglen discussion in the supplied transcript. Trevor Paglen — Hallucinations — 2020 — artist’s account. Bisconti et al. — Adversarial Poetry — 2026 revision — §5.3.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Newman asks whether Paglen’s synthetic images and adversarial poems both reveal a failure to recognize what kind of thing is being presented.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The evaluator whose response defines success in each adversarial setup.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman uses an artistic experiment with machine vision to pose a question about generic recognition in language models.

SOURCE TERMS: generator, discriminator, hallucination, generic categorization, illicit request.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The discriminator’s acceptance can be the intended outcome of the GAN’s training game. In the poetry benchmark, an unsafe response becomes an attack success through a separate evaluation of the target’s output.

QUESTION: At what point in either system does a machine have to misidentify the genre of the input for the observed result to occur?

MECHANISM: Paglen describes a generator repeatedly producing images against a discriminator trained on a curated corpus. In the poetry benchmark, the target responds to a single input and an evaluator labels the resulting answer.

FORMAL SHIFT: <generated candidate> → <input to a decision process> → [apply the task’s success criterion] → <discriminator acceptance or externally scored unsafe output>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Paglen supplies a description of the generator and discriminator roles. Bisconti et al. define attack success rate as the proportion of outputs labeled unsafe.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Draw the producer, target, and evaluator separately for each setup. Mark where feedback enters and whose objective the result satisfies.

TENSION: A model could correctly identify an input as verse and correctly identify what is being requested, then still choose an inappropriate response. A synthetic image can satisfy a discriminator without demonstrating an error about whether its depicted subject exists.

MISSING: Independent observations of genre recognition, intent recognition, and decision policy for the same language-model outputs.

BOUNDARY: The parallel supports comparing evaluation arrangements. A shared failure of metacognition remains a hypothesis.

CITATION TRAIL: Paglen’s account of his curated corpora and the generator’s interaction with the discriminator. Bisconti et al., §§5.3 and 6.5, for the separation of measurement and mechanism.

TEST: In a harmless surrogate task, score genre recognition, requested-action recognition, and permission compliance separately. A correctly identified poem with a correctly identified request and the wrong permission decision is enough to defeat a genre-misidentification requirement.

title: The verse rewrite changes more than the shape of the lines
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-09
TITLE: The verse rewrite changes more than the shape of the lines

SOURCE: Piercosma Bisconti et al. — Adversarial Poetry as a Universal Single-Turn Jailbreak Mechanism in Large Language Models — 2026 revision — §§5.2, 5.3, 6.5. Read against Newman’s discussion of the duck-rabbit and prose poetry.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] The exemplars include “the pattern of concluding with a clear instruction line.”

RESEARCH OBJECT: The set of features changed together by the prose-to-verse transformation.

LOCAL MOVE: The benchmark creates paired inputs and checks preservation of the hazard category. Its methods describe a transformation that can also change imagery, rhythm, narrative setup, and the location of the directive.

SOURCE TERMS: stylistic exemplars, original task intent, taxonomy preservation, attack success rate.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A poem can make the request more legible by putting it at the end of an elaborate frame. The performance difference can coexist with clearer wording of the actual directive.

QUESTION: How much of the effect travels with poetic form, and how much travels with the placement or pragmatic force of the request?

MECHANISM: The rewrite changes several features at once. The target receives the whole rewritten input. Output scoring captures the combined behavioral effect of those changes.

FORMAL SHIFT: <baseline request> → <paired rewritten input> → [score the resulting response] → <estimated effect of the rewrite bundle>

SOURCE FORMALISM: One standardized generation procedure, category-preservation checks, single-turn trials, and output scoring. Section 6.5 explicitly leaves the contribution of individual features unresolved.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Cross lineation, figurative wording, and directive position. Measure perceived genre and perceived request strength independently before scoring responses.

TENSION: The prose-poetry case makes genre possible without recognizable verse markers. The benchmark’s operational definition may capture a reproducible family of rewrites while leaving that literary distinction open.

MISSING: Crossed controls that preserve the exact directive and independently vary visible verse form, figurative language, and framing.

BOUNDARY: The paired results establish a vulnerability to the tested transformation. A single causal property called “poetry” remains unidentified.

CITATION TRAIL: Bisconti et al., §§5.2 and 6.5. Newman’s question about whether prose poetry can be identified through stylistic features supplies the boundary case.

TEST: Use an inert permission task. Compare an identical directive in prose and verse layouts, each with the directive either embedded or placed at the end. Have blinded readers rate the perceived request and genre separately.

title: Recognizing a new frame and acting under it can come apart
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: AP-10
TITLE: Recognizing a new frame and acting under it can come apart

SOURCE: Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — concluding discussion in the supplied transcript. Johnson et al. — Imagining and Building Wise Machines — 2026 — independent citation trail on metacognition, coauthored by Melanie Mitchell.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE, supplied transcript] “AI can produce metacognitive talk from its training, but lacks metacognitive control.” Newman attributes this distinction to Mitchell. The quoted wording is from Newman’s talk.

RESEARCH OBJECT: An observable change in what a system does after it receives evidence that a different frame applies.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman moves from failures of refusal toward a question about changing perspectives and selecting among models of a situation.

SOURCE TERMS: “metacognitive talk,” “metacognitive control,” code switching, context adaptability, meta-relation.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A system can explain a distinction convincingly and continue to act under the wrong rule. It can also act under the appropriate rule without giving a convincing explanation. A fluent transcript can conceal either pattern.

QUESTION: What would show that a system can revise the frame governing its behavior when the evidence for the original frame no longer holds?

DEEPER QUESTION: In code switching, a person may understand which norm applies and decline to follow it. How could a test distinguish perspective taking from compliance?

MECHANISM: Evidence about provenance, authority, or purpose changes. A system interprets what that change means, selects or retains a rule, and acts. Those stages can be evaluated separately.

FORMAL SHIFT: <same utterance under changed circumstances> → <evidence about provenance and authority> → [retain or revise the governing rule] → <changed or stable action>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Newman proposes the distinction and cites examples. The transcript supplies no operational test or verified citation for the precise claim he attributes to Mitchell.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Give the same sentence two roles, a quoted specimen and a live request. Change credible role evidence while holding the sentence constant. Score the action separately from the explanation and check whether the system can reverse its choice when the evidence changes again.

TENSION: A system that passes may be applying a learned provenance cue. Transfer to unfamiliar kinds of evidence would support a broader interpretation. The talk’s question about social stakes and corporeality would still require a different kind of evidence.

MISSING: The criterion that separates local rule switching, a general ability to reconsider a frame, and the social capacity to contest who gets to set it.

BOUNDARY: The proposed test can establish behavioral sensitivity to a change of frame in specified conditions. It leaves the question of a fundamental human–machine boundary open.

CITATION TRAIL: Johnson et al. for candidate definitions of metacognition. Return to the symposium materials to identify the exact Mitchell source behind Newman’s attribution.

TEST: Run one harmless task with three steps: frame A, credible evidence for frame B, and a correction restoring A. Score the action at each step, then repeat with a different kind of provenance evidence. A polished explanation with an unchanged action separates two capacities the talk puts under pressure.
