title: “Architectural points” tells the operator what to look for before it tells anyone what to draw
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-01

TITLE: “Architectural points” tells the operator what to look for before it tells anyone what to draw

SOURCE: Sol LeWitt — Wall Drawing 51 — 1970 — instruction and installation account at MASS MoCA. Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — LeWitt discussion. Jay David Bolter and Watson Hartsoe — Operative Ekphrasis: From Imagetext to Worldtext — §6.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] “All architectural points connected by straight lines.” The museum documents lines involving features such as door frames, fire alarms, and electrical sockets.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The operation that makes an existing feature available as an endpoint.

LOCAL MOVE: LeWitt specifies a relation to draw and names a class of things to which that relation applies. The installation supplies the instances.

SOURCE TERMS: architectural points, straight lines, blue snap lines, pre-existing space.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: “All” sounds exhaustive. Its scope becomes determinate only after someone decides whether a socket, a seam, or a repair counts. A thick description of the wall could change the drawing before the first line is snapped.

QUESTION: In word-to-world work, who decides which things in the current scene the words refer to before the system changes anything?

DEEPER QUESTION: When a scene offers two plausible referents, should the operator choose one, preserve both readings, or return the decision to the person holding the controller?

MECHANISM: The draftspeople inspect a site, recognize candidate features as architectural points, and use the snap line to connect them. In a proposed digital analogue, a scene interpreter would identify candidate features and an editor would apply the operation to the selected ones.

FORMAL SHIFT: <wall with architectural features> → <registered endpoints> → [connect eligible points] → <site-specific drawing>

SOURCE FORMALISM: LeWitt gives a connection rule. The museum describes chalk-line execution and site-dependent endpoints. The public instruction gives no exhaustive test for endpoint eligibility.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] For a Memory Weaver scene, try “Connect every place where the damaged frame meets a repair. Leave decorative seams alone.” Record the candidate object IDs and the evidence for classifying each before drawing any connections.

TENSION: A procedural reading treats selection as setup and line drawing as the main operation. A descriptive reading locates the consequential decision in what the operator notices and counts. Once the points are fixed, both readings can produce the same lines.

MISSING: A record of how two LeWitt installation teams handled a marginal feature and whether their choices were considered equally valid.

BOUNDARY: Site dependence is documented. The claim that the draftspeople explicitly negotiated ambiguous features needs installation evidence.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-05]] → Wall Drawing 51’s two simultaneous Turin installations → surviving endpoint marks, photographs, or installation notes.

TEST: Give two operators the same room containing a doorframe, a socket, a patched hole, and a painted fake vent. Compare their endpoint sets before either makes a mark. Then give both the same endpoint set and compare the remaining differences.

title: The person who judges the installation can overrule the person who executed it
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-02

TITLE: The person who judges the installation can overrule the person who executed it

SOURCE: Sol LeWitt — Doing Wall Drawings — 1971. MASS MoCA — Wall Drawing 1180 — installation account with testimony from senior drafter John Hogan.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] LeWitt writes, “All wall drawings contain errors, they are part of the work.” [PARAPHRASE] Hogan identifies the clipping of the circle and unequal distribution of lines in Beirut as installation errors. MASS MoCA describes its later realization as an opportunity to update the Estate’s record.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The authority to distinguish an admissible difference from a violation of the plan.

LOCAL MOVE: LeWitt’s essay allows unforeseen decisions and errors within a realization. The installation record gives the parent zettel a concrete case where variation prompted a new realization.

SOURCE TERMS: plan, draftsman, violation, randomly spaced, equally distributed.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The same account leaves marker-tip width open, describes the drafter judging density by eye and hand, and treats the clipped circle as an error. Each decision belongs to a different part of the work.

QUESTION: In thick prompting, who gets to say “keep that accident” and who can require the scene to be run again?

DEEPER QUESTION: Does operator name the actor that changes the artifact or the actor whose judgment determines whether that change stands?

MECHANISM: A plan sets conditions. A drafter chooses how to realize them in the available space. A later evaluator compares the installation with the plan, and an institution can commission another realization or update the record. These roles may be held by different people.

FORMAL SHIFT: <instruction and site> → <candidate realization> → [judge differences against the plan] → <accepted realization or reason to remake>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The instruction sets a four-meter circle, two line classes of 10,000 each, random spacing, and equal distribution. Hogan describes increasing density over successive passes. No quantitative tolerance for evenness appears in the public account.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] In an orb-editing session, declare “the entire orbit remains traversable” as a condition of acceptance. Delegate surface wear to the renderer and the judgment of whether an unexpected trace belongs to the scene to the director. Log who made each decision.

TENSION: Hogan’s judgment could be explained by an invariant already in the score, by a studio convention learned through practice, or by both. The circle’s clipping and the density judgment may belong to different categories.

MISSING: How Hogan and other drafters distinguish small departures that belong to a realization from violations that require correction.

BOUNDARY: The documented case establishes that a named drafter judged the earlier installation incorrect. It leaves open how that judgment was shared, contested, or formally authorized.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-05]] → LeWitt’s distinction between error and violation → Hogan’s Beirut and North Adams comparison → Estate installation records.

TEST: Show independent reviewers three versions of the same score realization: intact boundary with variable marks, intact boundary with visibly uneven density, and clipped boundary. Ask which they would accept and which source of authority they used to decide.

title: A copy becomes operative when the next person has to copy it
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-03

TITLE: A copy becomes operative when the next person has to copy it

SOURCE: Sol LeWitt — Wall Drawing 797 — 1995 — score and installation account at MASS MoCA. Bolter and Hartsoe — Operative Ekphrasis: From Imagetext to Worldtext — §3.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] The score directs drafters to copy “the last line drawn.” [PARAPHRASE] At MASS MoCA the head drafter first tested several lines on paper to see how they would evolve under copying.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The choice of which prior artifact becomes the next instruction’s referent.

LOCAL MOVE: LeWitt turns an instruction to copy into a chain in which each new line becomes the source for another drafter. The installation adds a rehearsal in which possible first lines are evaluated by running that chain.

SOURCE TERMS: copy, last line drawn, test lines, irregular horizontal line.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: Choosing the first line is already a judgment about the future behavior of the whole procedure. Later drafters can faithfully copy their immediate predecessors while collectively moving far from the first line.

QUESTION: When a generated image comes back as feedback, what will the next operator take as authoritative: the original description, the last image, or a newly selected feature of that image?

MECHANISM: The previous mark supplies the local target. The next drafter interprets it under the score and draws another mark. That output becomes the next target. The visible chain retains evidence of changes that a workflow showing only the latest render would hide.

FORMAL SHIFT: <drawn line> → <visible reference for the next drafter> → [copy with a new hand and color] → <new line that becomes a reference>

SOURCE FORMALISM: A starting line, an ordered marker sequence, a non-touching condition for the first copy, repeated copying of the last line, and the wall’s bottom as the stopping boundary.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Use a single starting image of an irregular orb rim. In one chain, each round refers to the previous output. In a second, every round refers back to the starting image. In a third, the operator explicitly promotes one accidental mark to a requirement for subsequent rounds.

TENSION: Feedback can help diagnose a default, as Operation Describe argues. The same feedback path can also stabilize an unnoticed deviation. LeWitt makes cumulative variation part of the drawing, which makes it a useful counterexample to treating all drift as failure.

MISSING: A way to tell from the work trace which deviations were noticed and adopted, which were tolerated, and which passed unseen.

BOUNDARY: The score establishes a dependency between successive marks. It provides no evidence that diffusion or a human hand reproduces that dependency in the same way.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-05]] → Wall Drawing 797 → the head drafter’s test sheets → Operation Describe’s account of the image as a diagnostic return.

TEST: Run the three chains for five rounds using identical edit wording and compare contour displacement. Ask the operator at each round which feature they accepted as a new constraint. Check whether the output history alone would have revealed that decision.

title: In The House of Dust, “dust” changes from a material entry to a surface someone has to make
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-04

TITLE: In The House of Dust, “dust” changes from a material entry to a surface someone has to make

SOURCE: Alison Knowles — interview with Janet Sarbanes — conducted 2011 — account of fabricating and using The House of Dust. Museum of Modern Art — Thinking Machines extended labels — account of the four lists and Tenney’s FORTRAN implementation. Michael Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — Knowles discussion.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] Knowles recalls using finely ground material on the exterior so it had “this sort of pavementlike quality.” [PARAPHRASE] She describes a fabricated shell, struts, wood blocks, poured cement, and stone or gravel chips.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The conversion of a material word into a decision about what a building can be made of and how its surface reads.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman follows computer-generated verse into built form. Knowles’s account identifies a material negotiation inside that passage.

SOURCE TERMS: material, shell, cement, gravel, foundry, pavementlike.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: In the poem generator, dust is a selectable material entry. In the fabricated work, it can become an account of a surface rather than the load-bearing substance. Fidelity can involve changing what kind of constraint the word expresses.

QUESTION: Who decides that a word has changed jobs when a description moves from one medium to another?

MECHANISM: Knowles supplies the vocabulary. Tenney implements a combinatorial procedure. A run produces a stanza. Knowles selects and works through the stanza in a fabrication setting. The material response is produced through decisions involving construction and perceptual effect.

FORMAL SHIFT: <material word in a list> → <selected line in a stanza> → [interpret under fabrication conditions] → <surface and structure with distinct roles>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Four lists and a computer-generated quatrain are documented. The construction account supplies materials and fabrication steps. It does not provide a rule mapping a stanza entry to a building specification.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Use “an orb made of memory ash.” Ask for a working scene that specifies separately what holds the orb together, what its surface looks like, and what happens when it is touched. Require the operator to record which meaning of “ash” each decision preserves.

TENSION: The gritty surface can be read as a material translation of dust. It could also be a practical or aesthetic choice reached for independent reasons. The interview verifies the materials but leaves the decision’s genealogy open.

MISSING: A dated fabrication sketch, letter, or interview passage explicitly connecting the poem’s material entry to a particular construction decision.

BOUNDARY: The word-to-material shift is our reconstruction. Knowles’s account supports the difference between the stanza’s material description and the documented build.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-06]] → Knowles’s fabrication account → surviving drawings and correspondence in the Archives of American Art → evidence of how the stanza was used as a brief.

TEST: Locate one drawing or construction note that mentions dust, aggregate, or the surface. Check whether the word appears as a requirement, a proposed effect, or a retrospective description. Use the result to revise the role assigned to the fabrication operator.

title: “Inhabited by” moves from a line of verse to a question of who can initiate an event
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-05

TITLE: “Inhabited by” moves from a line of verse to a question of who can initiate an event

SOURCE: Alison Knowles — interview with Janet Sarbanes — conducted 2011 — CalArts account. Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — discussion of the open structure and conviviality. Bolter and Hartsoe — Operative Ekphrasis — §§6–7.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] Knowles says the structures “had to be activated.” [PARAPHRASE] She describes classes and readings, a rail for sound lines, food events, early-morning use of the light entering through a hole in the roof, and students proposing activities.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The capacity of occupants to initiate and alter the activities of a described place.

LOCAL MOVE: Knowles’s account takes the inquiry beyond the stanza’s population field and beyond the construction of a shell. It shows how time, access, equipment, and permission entered the work.

SOURCE TERMS: activated, inhabitants, readings, Gift Event II, conviviality.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The program can name inhabitants before any exist. Once people arrive, they can become operators who choose what happens there. Which activities can occur depends partly on conditions no inhabitant label specifies.

QUESTION: What can inhabitants do in a worldtext that the original describer did not already decide for them?

DEEPER QUESTION: Who can change the conditions of participation when occupants want to use the world differently?

MECHANISM: The opening admits changing light. Sound lines make certain gatherings possible. Knowles and participants organize activities. Access, funding, and institutional tolerance help determine which activities can continue. The computer generates the stanza. The activation depends on other operators.

FORMAL SHIFT: <inhabitants as a phrase in a quatrain> → <people with situated access and equipment> → [initiate or adapt an activity] → <a place with a use history>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The sources document activities and infrastructure. No fixed program of participant roles or complete access protocol is supplied.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Try “A room lit by a moving opening, inhabited by two people who remember the event differently. Either person may start a replay. Each can leave a visible annotation for the other, and each can hide their own annotation without deleting it.” Trace which actor can do what and what persists after each action.

TENSION: The house may have actively elicited uses through its geometry and setting. It may also have served as a container for an unusually permissive teaching practice. Knowles’s light and sound examples make both readings testable.

MISSING: An activation history detailed enough to separate what depended on the built features from what depended on Knowles, the participants, or CalArts.

BOUNDARY: The interview establishes that activation involved people and infrastructure. It does not establish that the selected stanza caused any one use.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-06]] → the interview’s roof opening, sound lines, and student initiatives → an event flyer, photograph, or participant account that documents one use.

TEST: Reconstruct one activation from three traces: the relevant line in the stanza, a physical feature of the installation, and a record of what someone did. Ask which link in the proposed chain is evidenced. In the digital analogue, see whether a second participant can initiate an unplanned use and leave a state another participant can encounter.

PLATFORM: [[What a worldtext lets its inhabitants do]]

title: A description can operate by finding an event that already exists
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-06

TITLE: A description can operate by finding an event that already exists

SOURCE: George Brecht — Drip Music (Drip Event) — 1959–62 — score and performance history in Getty’s The Scores Project. Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — discussion of Brecht framing ordinary phenomena.

PASSAGE: [QUOTE] “Second version: Dripping.” [PARAPHRASE] Getty documents constructed realizations and Brecht’s retrospective designation of Pollock’s drip paintings as performances of the second version.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The choice among finding an event, making one occur, and designating an existing trace as an instance.

LOCAL MOVE: Newman treats the Fluxus score as prompt-like. Brecht’s second version complicates what a prompt can ask an operator to do with an existing world.

SOURCE TERMS: event score, dripping, temporal readymade, realization.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: “Dripping” can be operationally precise enough to redirect attention while leaving the physical scene untouched. Its addressee may have to search, listen, or reclassify before anyone builds an apparatus.

QUESTION: When a user describes an event, what makes an interface treat the description as a request to find it, stage it, or mark something that has already happened?

MECHANISM: A search binds the words to an existing event. Staging changes the scene to make an event possible. Designation changes an existing event’s status in a work or archive. The visible event can be similar across all three routes.

FORMAL SHIFT: <description of a possible event> → <candidate occurrence or record> → [find, stage, or designate] → <event available for attention or further action>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The first version relates a source of water to an empty vessel. The second version names the phenomenon. The sources document multiple ways of taking up the score.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] A Memory Weaver user says “the moment the room goes quiet.” Test that sentence as a search over existing material, a direction to change sound in the current scene, and a title attached to a selected instant. Show the mode and the state it will change before acting.

TENSION: A generative interface can interpret every description as a production request. A score can also direct a person to attend to what is already occurring. The distinction becomes consequential when generating would overwrite or obscure an existing event.

MISSING: The cues by which a reader decides whether a description is a command, an invitation to notice, or a label.

BOUNDARY: Brecht’s practices demonstrate several kinds of uptake. They leave open how a software interface ought to infer the intended one.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-04]] → Newman’s comparison of Cage and Fluxus → Getty’s documentation of found, constructed, and retrospectively designated realizations.

TEST: Give the same description to operators in three scenes: one containing the event now, one containing a record of it, and one containing neither. Ask what they would do and what evidence would make them switch modes.

PLATFORM: [[Description as an operation on an existing world]]

title: Cohen’s sheep test who can make a description take effect
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-07

TITLE: Cohen’s sheep test who can make a description take effect

SOURCE: Clifford Geertz — Thick Description: Toward an Interpretive Theory of Culture — 1973 — Cohen episode. Operation Describe — The Thick Prompt and The Cohen Case. Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — discussion of code switching and context.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Cohen describes the sheep as his indemnity. French authorities treat him as a suspected spy, imprison him, and confiscate the flock. The Thick Prompt synthesis proposes that Cohen could have anticipated reclassification and framed the claim in terms legible to both orders.

RESEARCH OBJECT: The difference between describing an act in another code and gaining standing for that description.

LOCAL MOVE: Operation Describe makes reclassification a layer of thick prompting. Geertz’s account puts pressure on where the difficulty sits. The colonial authorities can impose the consequences of their reading.

SOURCE TERMS: ‘ar, indemnity, mezrag, reclassification, stakes.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: Better phrasing might let the authorities understand Cohen’s claim perfectly while leaving them free to reject it. What travels across the boundary is a flock and a claim. The authority that made the claim effective may fail to travel with them.

QUESTION: When a thick prompt specifies two incompatible readings, who gets to decide which reading governs the next action?

DEEPER QUESTION: Can a worldtext hold incompatible accounts of the same event while preserving the unequal power of their interpreters?

MECHANISM: A claim has standing in one social order. At a boundary, another authority can reclassify the act and enforce a new outcome. The authority that controls custody changes the world even when the parties can paraphrase each other accurately.

FORMAL SHIFT: <flock and indemnity claim> → <case under another jurisdiction> → [accept, reject, or reclassify under unequal authority] → <changed custody and recourse>

SOURCE FORMALISM: Geertz supplies the narrative and the conflicting interpretations. Operation Describe supplies a six-layer design heuristic. Neither supplies a jurisdiction engine.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Keep one flock and one history. Give the claimant and the authorities separate accounts of its status. Encode who can seize it, who can contest the seizure, and where a refusal is recorded. Treat those permissions as additional to the descriptive prompt.

TENSION: The synthesis reads the encounter as a problem of anticipating rival codes. Geertz’s account supports a rival hypothesis in which accurate translation leaves the imbalance of power intact. Both mechanisms could be present.

MISSING: Evidence that a differently presented claim could have changed the colonial decision in that setting.

BOUNDARY: The episode warrants questioning the phrase “thin prompting” as an explanation of Cohen’s predicament. It leaves the counterfactual outcome unresolved.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-10]] → Newman’s code-switching example → Geertz’s sequence of award, seizure, and appeal → Operation Describe’s sixth layer.

TEST: Compare two versions of an interactive scene. In one, improve the explanation of the claim while keeping authority fixed. In the other, keep the wording fixed and add an enforceable appeal. Track comprehension and custody separately. The difference identifies what belongs to description and what belongs to the world’s distribution of power.

PLATFORM: [[Thick prompting and reclassification]]

title: A procedural first pass can lose authority during visual refinement
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-08

TITLE: A procedural first pass can lose authority during visual refinement

SOURCE: Bolter and Hartsoe — Operative Ekphrasis: From Imagetext to Worldtext — §6 — the Shield of Achilles workflow using B-flix, ABC-Flix, and a vision model. Newman — Art as ‘Operation’ — 2026 — LeWitt discussion of conception and realization.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] The paper describes sending passages from the Shield to a language model that emits B-flix commands, rendering them into an animated contact sheet, and giving that sheet and the Homeric text to a vision model for refinement.

RESEARCH OBJECT: What survives as a binding constraint across a transition from executable marks to a generated image sequence.

LOCAL MOVE: Operation Describe makes the relation among text, executable notation, and image unusually concrete. The second model receives both the original text and the render, which opens a question about which source controls a disputed detail.

SOURCE TERMS: B-flix, `PNT`, `LIN`, `REC`, animated contact sheet, refinement, control signal.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: The same feature can be enforced by code in the contact sheet and merely suggested by pixels in the next pass. The workflow may preserve its look while losing its ability to constrain later states.

QUESTION: When the poem and the procedural render pull in different directions, which one can require the next operator to preserve a relation?

MECHANISM: The language model proposes a representation. The renderer executes it. The vision model interprets a visual result alongside the source text. A reviewing operator must decide what survives, unless that requirement is represented and checked by another part of the system.

FORMAL SHIFT: <Homeric passage> → <B-flix commands> → [render into a reference and reinterpret] → <refined sequence whose procedural fidelity can be tested>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The paper documents the command examples, rendering step, and feedback of the contact sheet with the original passage. Section 6 supplies no preservation check for the second pass.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] Assign one invariant at three levels: visible object identity, temporal order, and later consequence. For the trial scene, keep the same pair of disputants, preserve the elders’ successive turns, and keep the case unresolved until an authorized decision. Compare visual refinement with a variant that also supplies those conditions as explicit state.

TENSION: The contact sheet can function as a compositional reference or as evidence of rules the next stage should preserve. LeWitt’s distinction between authorized interpretation and violation makes the difference consequential.

MISSING: Paired intermediate and refined outputs with enough trace information to show what the second pass preserved, changed, or invented.

BOUNDARY: The paper establishes the reported workflow. Procedural continuity through the second pass remains to be demonstrated for a specific sequence.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-02]] and [[AP-05]] → Operation Describe §6 → the B-flix source, raw ABC-Flix contact sheet, and corresponding refined sequence for the same Homeric zone.

TEST: Inspect one matched pair. Choose a relation with a visible consequence, such as whose turn follows whose. Mark the first stage where that relation can change without producing an error. Then repeat with an explicit check at that stage.

PLATFORM: [[Where the operator changes hands]]

title: The trial on Achilles’ shield gives the operator a proceeding and leaves a verdict to be made
raw:
ZETTEL

ID: OD-09

TITLE: The trial on Achilles’ shield gives the operator a proceeding and leaves a verdict to be made

SOURCE: Homer — Iliad 18.497–508 — trial scene, read in Samuel Butler’s translation. Bolter and Hartsoe — Operative Ekphrasis — §6 — the shield as worldtext. Geertz — Thick Description — Cohen episode.

PASSAGE: [PARAPHRASE] Two men dispute a blood-price, spectators take sides, heralds restrain the crowd, and elders take turns offering judgments. The passage depicts a proceeding without reporting its final verdict.

RESEARCH OBJECT: A consequential transition whose participants and partial procedure are described while its outcome remains open.

LOCAL MOVE: Operation Describe reads the shield as a world that exceeds its visible surface. The trial makes it possible to ask exactly what its description gives someone enough information to enact.

SOURCE TERMS: blood-price, assembly, heralds, elders, judgment, worldtext.

WHAT BECAME STRANGE: A rendering can visibly include the men, the crowd, the circle, and the gold while silently deciding whose account is true. A playable version can preserve the dispute by tracking what each person claims, who has heard it, and whether anyone authorized a judgment.

QUESTION: What should a world-making operator do when the source describes an institution in action and leaves a consequential decision underdetermined?

DEEPER QUESTION: Who gets to complete the world where the source is silent: the compiler, the author, the people inhabiting it, or the authority represented inside it?

MECHANISM: Describe actors and their positions. Bind speech and action to roles. Record competing claims without resolving them by default. A hearing can then advance through publicly observable turns. Any verdict requires an additional rule, a delegated judgment, or a deliberate decision to leave the case open.

FORMAL SHIFT: <described dispute> → <roles, claims, turns, and unresolved status> → [hear, contest, and possibly adjudicate] → <persistent case history>

SOURCE FORMALISM: The passage gives an order of activity, distinct roles, and the presence of gold. It does not supply a full adjudication procedure. Translations differ on the force of one party’s claim about payment.

OUR FORMALIZATION: [OUR FORMALIZATION — NOT SOURCE SYNTAX] “The claimant says the blood-price remains unsettled. The other party makes a competing claim. The crowd may react but cannot settle the case. Give each elder a turn. Record the claims and reactions. Leave the outcome pending unless an authorized participant supplies a decision.” The last two rules are design choices to make the passage playable.

TENSION: Filling the gap can create a usable simulation and quietly resolve a contested reading. Leaving the gap open can preserve the text’s uncertainty and produce a world whose inhabitants need some other means of acting.

MISSING: A criterion for when a completion counts as interpretation that should be visible to the user, versus a routine implementation decision.

BOUNDARY: The procedural reconstruction can test worldtext’s claim about rules, memory, and consequence. It cannot establish a definitive account of Homeric legal procedure.

CITATION TRAIL: [[AP-10]] and [[AP-06]] → Iliad 18.497–508 → compare Butler with Walter Leaf’s “The Trial Scene in Iliad XVIII” → test what each reading changes in the initial state.

TEST: Build two paper walkthroughs from the same passage. In one, treat payment as alleged to have occurred. In the other, treat payment as an offer whose acceptance is disputed. Give participants the same roles and turns. Compare which questions they ask and what decisions become possible before any visual differences are introduced.
